meta.title: Who really said "If people cannot write well, they cannot think well"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not found in Orwell. The attribution traces to university president John H. Bunzel in the mid-1970s, quoted without a source. Orwell wrote something genuinely close in 'Politics and the English Language' — and it is better.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If people cannot write well, they cannot think well'?
meta.ogDescription: No Orwell source. Attributed to him by John H. Bunzel in the 1970s, uncited. The real Orwell line on language and thought is in 'Politics and the English Language' (1946).

answer.label: Not sourced to Orwell — origin unknown
answer.sourceLine: The sentence is not in Orwell’s essays, novels, letters or journalism. The trail leads instead to John H. Bunzel, then president of San José State University, who attributed it to Orwell in the mid-1970s without citing anything — the firmly citable instance being a 1977 book that quotes him. Orwell did write about the link between sloppy language and sloppy thought, and that passage is both real and sharper.

source.heading: What Orwell actually wrote

docMeta.dd: Quoted in a 1977 book (an earlier 1976 appearance is reported, unverified)

source.excerpt: But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought. A bad usage can spread by tradition and imitation even among people who should and do know better.
trail: The sentence appears nowhere in Orwell’s corpus. Wikiquote files it under disputed, recording that it was attributed to him by John H. Bunzel and ‘not found in Orwell’s works or in reports contemporaneous with his life’ Wikiquote ↗.

The solidly citable instance is a 1977 book quoting Bunzel. An earlier Bunzel appearance in a 1976 periodical is reported from a search snippet; we have not inspected it, so we date the attribution ‘mid-1970s’ rather than assert 1976.

The genuine Orwell material is in ‘Politics and the English Language’ (April 1946), which argues the relationship in both directions — and in Nineteen Eighty-Four, whose Newspeak exists precisely to make heretical thought impossible for want of words sourced quotations ↗.
source.excerptNote: Orwell’s actual formulation. Note that he makes it reciprocal — thought corrupts language and language corrupts thought — where the fake runs in one direction only, toward a tidy conclusion about who ends up doing your thinking.
source.rightsNote: The circulating sentence has no identified author, so there is nothing to clear — but it should not be presented as Orwell’s. For the genuine passage: Orwell died in 1950, so his work is public domain in the UK and EU since 1 January 2021, while US status varies by work and ‘Politics and the English Language’ (1946) remains protected there. The 1977 book that carries the misattribution is itself in copyright. Quote short, cite properly. This is not legal advice.

author.name: George Orwell
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Orwell
author.bio: George Orwell (1903–1950) wrote the single most-assigned essay in English on the relationship between language and thought. That makes any aphorism on the subject feel like his by default — and it means a sentence can be absorbed into his corpus simply by being about what he was famously about. This one has never had a source, only a resemblance.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: A paraphrase of a real Orwell argument has been promoted into a quotation from him — and, as often happens, the paraphrase is more emphatic and less careful than the original.

items.why: Absent from his published work and from anything reported in his lifetime. The attribution begins with a university president quoting it in the 1970s, citing nothing Wikiquote ↗.

Orwell’s point is reciprocal — bad thought produces bad language and bad language produces bad thought. The fake runs one way and lands on a conclusion about being colonised by other people’s thinking, which is punchier and not what he wrote.
The sentence also circulates credited to Wilde and to Woolf in near-identical wording — the signature of an orphan aphorism looking for a parent.

misattribution.truthLine: Not sourced to Orwell. Attributed to him by John H. Bunzel in the mid-1970s with no citation; the real Orwell argument is in ‘Politics and the English Language’ (1946) sourced text ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The chain it describes — can’t write, therefore can’t think, therefore someone thinks for you — is exactly the anxiety Nineteen Eighty-Four dramatises through Newspeak. That is why it passes as Orwell without inspection: it is a plausible summary of his politics.

But summary is the operative word. Orwell’s own version is more modest and more useful, because it allows that the corruption runs both ways and can be reversed by anyone willing to take some trouble over a sentence.
context.detailsSummary: The real Orwell on language and thought
detailsBody: ‘But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.’
‘It becomes ugly and inaccurate because our thoughts are foolish, but the slovenliness of our language makes it easier for us to have foolish thoughts.’
Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949): Newspeak is designed so that heretical thought is unthinkable for want of words.
The fake, as circulated: ‘…others will do their thinking for them’ — also seen under Oscar Wilde and Virginia Woolf.
context.pull: Orwell said the corruption runs both ways. The fake only runs one.
